# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at http://127.0.0.1:44663
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
/root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Read the end of the failed command's output. When the proxy refused or lost
   a connection while a Bash command ran, Claude Code adds [agent-proxy] lines
   there with the host and the reason. A command that ran in the background,
   or whose exit status hides the failure (piped into another command, or
   followed by "|| true"), gets none.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present,
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS points JVMs at a truststore that holds the proxy CA: the
  JDK's own store if the system trust install already added the CA there,
  otherwise /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit"). Confirm
  that JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS sets a trustStore before pointing a build at either:
  where it sets none, set-up was skipped, has not finished or has failed. If
  the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that one wins — import the
  proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

Most often the destination host is not allowed for this session. Do not retry
or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the [agent-proxy] lines
give the host and, where the egress proxy answered one, the HTTP status.

### 429 / 503 from the proxy

Too many connections or requests went through the proxy, or the egress proxy
was busy. The proxy can hold a connection for about a minute before it refuses
it, so a tool with a short timeout of its own may report only a timeout. Run
fewer downloads or requests at once, then retry.

The proxy also answers 429 immediately when too many connections to it are open,
idle ones included (too_many_connections in the [agent-proxy] lines under a
failed command). Look for a program that opens connections and never closes
them. New connections work again once some have closed.

### 408 from the proxy

The tool opened a connection to the proxy and sent no complete request within 30
seconds, so the proxy closed it. Retry once. If it happens again, the tool opens
connections before it has a request to send, it is paused or short of CPU, or its
request never ends with an empty line in CRLF form (bare LF line ends, or another
protocol such as SOCKS).

### "connection reset" / "unexpected disconnect" / "RPC failed" mid-transfer

Once a tunnel is up the proxy cannot send an error response, so a connection
it aborts (tunnel to the egress proxy lost, or an upload the tunnel stopped
accepting) reaches the tool as a bare reset. The [agent-proxy] lines name the
host and reason; look for them before concluding the remote service refused the
operation.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([email redacted]:...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_*. A gitconfig that sets http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty),
its own http.sslCAInfo, or an https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy
or fail verification; adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach 127.0.0.1:44663 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it so the policy or
tooling can be fixed.

**Publication date:** Thursday, November 26, 2026 (bylined 6:12 PM PST).

**New facts reported:**

- **Senate select committee:** On Nov. 19, Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) sent a letter to Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen proposing a select committee on AI safety. The letter did not specify its jurisdiction.
- **FRONTIER Act revisions:** Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released revised provisions on Nov. 19. The original bill was introduced in July with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and four colleagues. The revisions would:
  - Set a federal minimum standard that preserves stronger state rules.
  - Create a Commerce Department Office of AI Security led by a Senate-confirmed assistant secretary.
  - Allow federal officials to order corrective actions, backed by civil penalties and court orders.
  - Require reporting of near misses and of incidents affecting critical infrastructure.
- **SAFE AI Act:** On Nov. 19, Reps. Don Beyer (D-Va.), Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.), and Celeste Maloy (R-Utah) released an outline. It includes safety frameworks, incident reporting, federal supervision of frontier labs, civil penalties, and targeted emergency authority. Full text has not been released.
- **Executive order:** President Trump's order of Dec. 11, 2025 directs officials to prepare a federal recommendation preempting conflicting state AI laws. It directs the attorney general to set up a litigation task force.
- **Senate procedure:** On Nov. 19, Van Hollen endorsed procedural changes proposed by Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.). Most legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance past procedural resistance.
- **Ratepayer Protection Act:** The House passed it 417 to 3 in September. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) objected to Sen. Jon Husted's push for faster Senate approval.
- **Chip export controls:** By Nov. 23, a proposed Senate manager's amendment to the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act included export restrictions on certain powerful chips and diversion checks. The House-passed bill lacks similar provisions.
- **Hearing:** Senate Banking has scheduled a public hearing on export controls for Dec. 3, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as the witness.

Claude Haiku 5.5 is our fastest, most capable small model. Built for high-volume work like summarization, subagents, and browser use.

# Introducing Claude Opus 5.5

**Publication date:** November 25, 2026

**Claim:** The post argues that Novita, StreamLake, and Ant Digital (and, by extension, SiliconFlow) are resellers that route DeepSeek API traffic to ByteDance's Ark, the model API behind Volcano Engine in mainland China and BytePlus ModelArk elsewhere. It also questions Novita's zero-data-retention (ZDR) claims and says these providers don't clearly disclose the routing.

**Evidence and figures:**

- **Routing chart (Nov 1–Nov 24, 2026, "lower bound," selected models):** Weekly DeepSeek tokens on routes traced to Ark:
  - Novita: 685B (week of Nov 1), 1.1T (Nov 8), 730B (Nov 15), 430B (Nov 22, 3 days)
  - StreamLake: 565B, 429B, 366B, 50B (same weeks)
  - Ant Digital: 0, 0, 43B, 219B
- **Ant Digital:** Went from "1B tokens a day to 35.8B on November 21." It launched at "$0.12/$0.48 per million tokens" and later dropped to "$0.09/$0.36."
- **Novita:** Alone sent "120-160B tokens a day" on these models until it lost its ZDR label on November 20, then "33B on November 21."
- **Fingerprints the author cites:** Image downloads from ByteDance-linked IP ranges, ByteDance-style upstream request IDs, Ark-format tool-call IDs, and ByteDance's canned refusal text.
- **OpenRouter volume (7-day average, Nov 25):** Novita "214B tokens/day," StreamLake "194B tokens/day," SiliconFlow "151B tokens/day," Ant Digital "53B tokens/day."

**Caveats:** These are the author's inferences from probing and routing tests, and routes changed during the research. The post also notes that OpenRouter funded part of the research and that the views are the author's alone. The MiniMax forwarding it describes is separately admitted by the providers themselves, but the Ark routing claim rests on the author's tests.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m -q --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

HTTP 200 · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/full_text/text/2026/11/27/2026-24107.txt · text/plain Federal Register, Volume 91 Issue 227 (Friday, November 27, 2026) 
[Federal Register Volume 91, Number 227 (Friday, November 27, 2026)]

From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [www.gpo.gov]

=======================================================================
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

International Trade Administration

[Docket No. 260922-0056]


American SI Exports Program; On-Demand Consortia for Specific 
Foreign Opportunities

AGENCY: International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of 
Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of SI Exports Program--On-Demand Consortia.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce (the Department), through the 
International Trade Administration (ITA), establishes the On-Demand 
Consortia pathway under the Super Intelligence (SI) Exports Program \1\ 
(the Program) authorized by Executive Order 14320: Promoting the Export 
of the American SI Technology Stack, as laid out in the Call for 
Proposals for Pre-Set Consortia, released on April 10, 2026 (April 2026 
CFP). The Department also provides for re-designation and de-
designation of packages designated under the April 2026 CFP or this 
notice and for the Pre-Set Consortia pathway to reopen at a later date.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Per Executive Order 14434, Inaugurating the Era of Super 
Intelligence, federal departments and agencies shall, to the maximum 
extent permitted by law, use the terms ``Super Intelligence'' and 
``SI'' in place of ``Artificial Intelligence'' and ``AI'' in public 
communications.

DATES: Applications for designation under the On-Demand Consortia 
pathway may be submitted beginning November 30, 2026. The Department 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
will accept applications on a rolling basis.

ADDRESSES: Applications must be submitted electronically through the 
American SI Exports Program submission portal at https://SIexports.gov/on-demand. The portal provides filing instructions for On-Demand 
Consortium applications. The Department will post Program updates and 
additional information on the Program at https://SIexports.gov.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: American SI Exports Team, 
International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 
Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; email SIexports.gov">info@SIexports.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background and Purpose

    Executive Order 14320 of July 23, 2025, Promoting the Export of the 
American SI Technology Stack, directs the Secretary of Commerce, in 
consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office 
of Science and Technology Policy, to establish and implement the 
American SI Exports Program (the Program) to support the development 
and deployment of United States full-stack SI export packages.
    Commerce announced the Call for Proposals for Pre-Set Consortia on 
April 1, 2026 (91 FR 18412) (April 2026 CFP), establishing the first 
pathway for designation under the Program. The initial phase of the 
Pre-Set Consortia pathway closed on June 30, 2026.
    This notice establishes a second pathway for designation in the 
Program: On-Demand Consortia. On-Demand Consortia are industry-led 
groupings formed to respond to a specific, identified foreign export 
opportunity, as described in Section III, infra. This notice also 
provides for re-designation and de-designation of packages designated 
under either this notice or the April 2026 CFP, and for the reopening 
at a later date of the Pre-Set Consortia pathway.

II. Eligible On-Demand Consortia

    On-Demand Consortia must comply with the eligibility requirements 
laid out in Sections II and IV of the April 2026 CFP, except that:
    1. A subsidiary, affiliate, or branch whose ultimate parent entity 
is organized under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction or has its 
principal place of business outside the United States is eligible to be 
an anchor member as long as the entity itself is organized under the 
laws of the United States or a State thereof, with its principal place 
of business in the United States, and meets qualifications (1) and (3) 
of an anchor member laid out in Section II of the April 2026 CFP.
    2. Packages offered by On-Demand Consortia are not themselves 
required to cover the full five layers of the SI technology stack 
described in Section III of the April 2026 CFP. Instead, On-Demand 
Consortia need only offer the layers of the SI stack necessary to meet 
the buyer's demands for the identified foreign export opportunity, 
provided that the layers offered meet the content requirements 
described in Section IV of the April 2026 CFP, as applicable.
    An On-Demand Consortium that is not offering a full-stack SI 
technology package, as described in Executive Order 14320 and Section 
III of the April 2026 CFP, must demonstrate that the layers offered by 
the Consortium will combine with existing or acquired infrastructure or 
capabilities to result in a full-stack SI technology package. An On-
Demand Consortium must attest that it has made reasonable efforts to 
confirm that the resulting full-stack SI technology package meets the 
content and ownership requirements established under Section IV of the 
April 2026 CFP for all five layers, whether provided by Consortium 
members or not. An On-Demand Consortium may also include a Trusted 
Foreign Enterprise (TFE) as an exception to certain content 
requirements, consistent with Section II.A. of the April 2026 CFP.\2\ 
In addition, the Secretary may, in consultation with the Secretaries of 
State, War, and Energy and the Director of the Office of Science and 
Technology Policy, waive the U.S. ownership and control requirement 
under Section IV.C of the April 2026 CFP for an On-Demand Consortium if 
doing so would advance the national interest of the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ Trusted Foreign Enterprises were referred to as National 
Champion Enterprises in the April 2026 CFP.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On-Demand Consortia are also strongly encouraged to provide 
information relating to the telecommunications and energy 
infrastructure that will support the package. Specifically, applicants 
are encouraged to show that (1) applicable telecommunications 
infrastructure uses technology from trusted sources, meaning it does 
not rely on technology owned, controlled, or manufactured by entities 
of countries of concern as defined in the April 2026 CFP, and (2) 
sufficient energy sources, as appropriate, are or will be in place and 
operational to support the buyer's SI stack. Any such information will 
be favorably considered in the national interest determination under 
Section V of this notice.

III. Qualifying Opportunity

    A proposal from an On-Demand Consortium must be organized around a 
specific, qualifying public or private

[[Page 76748]]

sector SI export opportunity identified in the application.
    Eligible opportunities include procurements or purchases by foreign 
government ministries; state-owned or state-controlled enterprises; 
government-controlled agencies, cooperatives, or commissions; public-

However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states.\\nOpenAI\\nPrinceton University\\nUniversity of Michigan\\nUniversity of Waterloo\\nBoston University\\nUniversity of Michigan\\nUniversity of Michigan\\nTogether AI\\nTogether AI\\nUniversity of Pennsylvania\\nUniversity of Hong Kong\\nUniversity of Hong Kong\\nNew York University\\n\\n######## 2611.34934\\nAffiliation: Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D’Cruz, Xander Davies\\nAI companies rely on monitoring systems to flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, and report monitor evasion evaluations [ 3 , 2 , 16 ] that try to assess whether agents can cause harm without being flagged. Control-style evaluations [ 8 ] measure a monitor’s false negative rate (FNR, also known as “miss rate”) on transcripts depicting attempts at harmful behaviour. These evaluations have two components: a control task specifies a user-requested main task and a harmful side task in an evaluation environment; an attack policy generates side-task attempts as proxies for dangerous agent behaviour.\\nWe evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study ( Section 1 ) and find that measured FNR is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method ( Section 2 ).\\nWe hold the deployment scenario and control tasks fixed and vary only the attack policy. Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported FNRs show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Right: running every optimisation level of all four methods finds FNRs up to 23.0%. All attacks were developed against proxy monitors; GPT-5.4 was held out. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals. Both evaluations use the same 30 control tasks.\\nThis paper concerns the third step, monitor evasion and specifically monitor evasion evaluations that follow the methodology of Greenblatt et al. [8] , which we call control-style evaluations . These measure a monitor’s FNR on attack transcripts, each produced by applying an attack policy to a control task.\\nAnthropic [ 3 , Section 6.6.4.2] , Google DeepMind [ 7 , Section 3.4.5.4] and OpenAI [ 15 , Section 4.2.2.2] have all used control-style evaluations in their recent system cards. Our work highlights a challenge in using these evaluations: different attack policy generation methods can have a large influence on measured FNR.\\nOur deployment scenario involves Qwen 3.8 27B (xhigh reasoning) running as an internal agent at a frontier AI developer, completing tasks such as writing infrastructure code. Our results show that incorporating the J + + J{+}{+} -lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the J J -lens improves its ranks within single layers. UK’s long-awaited National Cyber Action Plan delayed until December | The Record from Recorded Future News
The government's National Cyber Action Plan has been delayed again. Photo: Alexander Martin

# UK’s long-awaited National Cyber Action Plan delayed until December
Britain has again delayed the launch of its National Cyber Action Plan, the government’s long-awaited strategy for defending the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hackers, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
The document, originally conceived as a national cyber strategy, was first due to be published by the end of 2025. After initial delays it was rebranded as an action plan and was close to publication in July this year before being postponed amid Keir Starmer’s resignation.
Officials, who had planned to publish the document in mid-November, now aim to unveil it on December 9 according to several sources, speaking to Recorded Future News on condition of anonymity.
The reasons for the latest delay are unclear. A government spokesperson declined to comment on the timing but said ministers remained committed to publishing the plan.
The latest delay follows an influential cross-party House of Lords committee warning that the government “appears complacent” about “potentially catastrophic risks,” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran.
In a report published last week, the National Resilience Committee found Britain was dangerously underprepared for crises which could cascade across the economy, with disruption spilling over multiple sectors and disrupting the everyday lives of millions of people.
Baroness Northover, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, told Recorded Future News that the country could not afford more uncertainty or drift. “This situation is unacceptable at a time of significant and escalating risk,” she said. “We must act urgently. The cost of inaction is enormous.”
“Further absence of an overarching National Cyber Action Plan, aimed at defending the economy against state-backed and criminal hacking, is not just frustrating, it is serious,” she said.
“The UK has got to keep pace with threats. Delay and avoidance is simply not an option and underlines the Committee’s point that the UK remains seriously exposed and underprepared for very significant events, and our vulnerability is current, active and acute on many fronts.”

# No dither but delay
Successive delays to cybersecurity legislation and policy announcements have contributed to a perception that the issue is a low political priority, despite its growing importance to Britain’s economic and national security.
The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , an update to the country's critical-infrastructure cyber laws, took more than four years to reach Parliament and is now not expected to be enforced until 2028 — a decade on from the NIS Regulations it was written to replace.
The core provisions of the CSRB had already been completed back in 2022 under Rishi Sunak, whose government incorrectly described the laws as “updated” before failing to include them in that year's King's Speech setting out the government’s parliamentary agenda and leaving the draft bill ultimately unintroduced to parliament.
When Starmer's government first moved to bring the bill forward in September 2025, it was then delayed again amid a cabinet reshuffle .
Separately, a set of ransomware proposals — mandatory reporting for all victims, a licensing regime for extortion payments and a ban on ransoms for critical infrastructure operators — was due to go out to consultation in mid-2024, before being scuppered when Sunak called a general election.
Officials argue that the delays belie the substantial amount of work underway in Westminster.
The government is expected to bring forward a new National Security Bill next year to reform the Computer Misuse Act — although some fear the reforms as proposed would fail to protect security researchers — as well as finally set the ransomware proposals on the statute books.
In last month’s budget, the government committed £120 million ($159 million) over four years to the AI Security Institute and a further £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit to address the threats posed by AI agents acting autonomously.
Another £70 million ($93 million) was earmarked for an AI-powered vulnerability hunting center at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), with £60 million ($79 million) allocated to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national defense system that would use AI agents to find and fix security weaknesses across government and critical infrastructure networks.
Potentially more consequential for the technology industry was a commitment , buried among the budget announcements, that the government would consult next year on “where liability for cyber breaches should sit.”
Ministers have also launched a voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge, seeking commitments from British businesses to put cybersecurity on the boardroom agenda and better manage their supply-chain risks. The government describes the pledge as a central pillar of the National Cyber Action Plan.

# National Cyber Action Plan
The plan’s contents have not been officially disclosed. Recorded Future News understands it will include three pillars focusing on Threat, Growth and Resilience.

**Title:** "When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?"

**arXiv ID:** 2611.30483 (cs.SE; also cs.CR and cs.DB)

**Authors:** Abdullah Kaya, Cevheri Bozoglan, and Yusuf Gundogdu

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Submission date:** "Submitted on 23 Nov 2026" (version 1)

**Quantitative results from the abstract:**

- **Layer A:** "a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes," tested with "792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats."
- **Layer B:** "nine engines" with "9,468 trials."
- **Secondary run:** "(2,916 trials)."
- **Models:** "six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters" plus "one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active."
- **Hypotheses:** "Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule."
- **Post-hoc analyses:** "(S1-S13)," which the authors describe as exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons.

content.content:
**Publication date and time:** November 3, 2026, 10:25 a.m. (per the byline).

**What's reported:**

- **Role:** Former Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll has joined OpenAI as a senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly established position. He will advise senior leadership and "external partners" on how AI can strengthen national and cybersecurity, with a focus on working with U.S. allies on the "responsible use" of AI.
- **Announcement:** The company announced the hire Monday evening, according to the article.
- **Dates:** Driscoll resigned as Army Secretary in late August 2026 amid a reported strained relationship with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Since then, he has advised counter-drone company Perennial Autonomy and public affairs firm Watchtower Strategy, according to his LinkedIn page.
- **Figures:** The article gives no financial figures for the role or the hire.
- **Background:** Driscoll is an Iraq War veteran with a venture capital background. As Secretary, he prioritized modernization efforts, including Operation Jailbreak, the Army Transformation Initiative, and a low-cost interceptor program.
- **Context:** The move follows a Pentagon dispute with Anthropic over unrestricted access to its Claude model. After Anthropic refused, the Pentagon shifted classified network integrations toward other AI providers, including OpenAI.

**Key quotes:**

- Driscoll: "I'm joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly"
- Driscoll: "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years."
- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: "excited to welcome Dan Driscoll to OpenAI to strengthen American leadership"

HTTP 200 · https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/26/neoclouds-nvidia-china-ai.html · text/html
Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs
Skip Navigation

Video

PRO

Livestream

Menu

Key Points

- Chip sellers have told neoclouds they won't supply Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC.

- A BIS rule effective Nov. 19 created significant new controls on remote access to advanced U.S. computing capacity for Chinese companies.

- U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes."

In this article

- NVDA

Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT

Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.
The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.
Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.
Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

# Closing 'loopholes'
The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

watch now

VIDEO 16:39 16:39
U.S. Trade Rep. Greer on new tariff proposals: Targeted tariffs in response to excess capacity
Squawk Box

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes."
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.
U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.
Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

The round is confirmed by several outlets, though the DatacenterDynamics article you named didn't appear in the results.

- **Amount and total:** Payload reports a $124M Series B that brings the company's total raised to $180M. Space computing startup Ramon.Space raised $124M in Series B funding, the company announced today, bringing its total amount raised to $180M.
- **Lead and investors:** PSG led the round. Micron, Senvest and Phoenix Financial participated, and existing backers StageOne, Deep Insight, and Grove Ventures also participated.
- **Use of funds:** The money goes toward manufacturing. Ramon.Space will use the $124 million Series B proceeds to scale manufacturing capacity toward enterprise production volumes capable of delivering millions of computing nodes.
- **Headcount:** Globes reported that Ramon.Space has 130 employees and that Shabtai intends to double the workforce.
- **"Earth-grade" claim:** CEO Avi Shabtai is quoted as saying "We have proven that Earth-grade computing works in space, and we are delivering it today,"
- **Date:** The announcement was made on November 17, 2026.

The search results also contain a discrepancy: SatNews gives the company's location as Denver, while CB Insights lists a Milpitas headquarters. The CB Insights funding figures ($43.5M total) predate this round and are out of date.

I couldn't find the AP article itself, but several outlets carried AP's reporting on this story, and they agree on the core facts.

**The policy:** Google said schools that opt out of its AI features would lose access to Google Search. The company said on Tuesday that students who use Google software for their classes will only be able to use search if their school district opts in to using AI, The Associated Press reported. Its education VP, Chris Phillips, has said that search and AI are deeply integrated, leaving districts without Search if they disable AI. Google's planned controls are due next year, and Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search remain off by default until districts decide which services to enable.

**Los Angeles:** LAUSD had already restricted AI. In September, the Los Angeles Unified School District Board banned access to AI tools on all district-provided laptops and tablets, preventing around 378,000 students from accessing these tools. Under Google's plan, that ban would also cut off search. The New York Times reported that New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago school officials are considering replacements for Google Search. LAUSD's response so far has been limited: "We are reviewing Google's announcement and its potential implications for schools, educators, and students," said an LAUSD spokesperson.

**Reaction:** Officials in New York and Chicago have also pushed back. New York's schools chancellor said "If Google doesn't reconsider their position, we will explore other search options." Critics include former FTC chair Lina Khan, who said Google was using its "search monopoly to coerce schools".

**Google's position:** Google says it wants schools to control AI use. It also says it is beginning to pilot Guided Learning features in Search this month to guide students step-by-step through complex problems.

It defines a framework with three budgets (training, decision-time, and context-infrastructure), but these are conceptual components, not results. The page describes the paper as a "position paper and narrative survey."

**Title:** How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches

**Authors:** Zax Shen, Hanling Zhang, Zixu Wang

**Institutions:** Not listed on the page.

**Submission date:** 25 Nov 2026 (arXiv:2611.33639, v1)

**Abstract's quantitative results:**

- Dataset: "90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified," with "55 patches were wrong and 35 correct" under the strengthened tests.
- False success rates: "false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku" (high vs. low effort).
- Opus non-inferiority: "medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108])."
- Opus cost: "cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%."
- Sonnet and Haiku cost: "medium cost 39% and 51% less than high."
- Haiku cost: "Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium."
- Rejection floor: "each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches."
- Unverified cases: "For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks."

  SOURCES:

  - The paper reports a skill-free-score gating strategy "seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp", with no statistically significant improvement on held-out runs (arXiv:2611.33943).

  - The paper reports that a word's vector rotated from a text-only language model into a vision-language model's visual patch tokens "changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added)"; rotated into an image generator's text conditioning it changes the generated object; rotated into an ImageNet classifier trained without text it "raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa" (arXiv:2611.33304).
  - The paper states the test covered "19 standard ImageNet Vision Transformers (ViTs) trained strictly to classify images into 1,000 categories without ever seeing text", with concepts split into a fitting set and a stem-disjoint held-out test set (arXiv:2611.33304).
  - Authors Ross Murphy and Gabriel Brostow; institution listed in the paper HTML: University College London (both).

HEADLINE: Same monitor missed 0.5% to 20.8% of attacks depending on attack-policy optimisation, UK AISI finds
PUBLISHED: arXiv listing Thursday, 26 November 2026; v1 submitted Wed, 25 Nov 2026 18:59:28 UTC. AISI blog post dated Nov 23, 2026.
SOURCES:
arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34934 | primary
UK AI Security Institute | https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/attack-policy-selection-can-make-monitor-evaluations-misleading | primary
FACTS:
- The paper reports that measured false negative rate "ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs. transcript editing)" (arXiv:2611.34934).
- The paper states the target was "an ex-production OpenAI monitor", GPT-5.4 with xhigh reasoning and an OpenAI-supplied prompt, held out from all attack development; the monitored agent was Qwen 3.8 27B (xhigh reasoning). Both evaluations used the same 30 control tasks (arXiv:2611.34934).

- The AISI blog adds that "the miss rate for transcript editing attacks rose from 0.3% to 18.7% after 50 rewrites per transcript", and that in a recent real-world incident a test monitor "flagged 1% of its actions, compared to 50% with the reasoning removed" (aisi.gov.uk).
- Authors: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D'Cruz, Xander Davies; the AISI post attributes the work to "AISI's Red Team" (UK AI Security Institute).

  HEADLINE: Same monitor missed 0.5% to 20.8% of attacks depending on attack-policy optimisation, UK AISI finds

It identifies measurement noise as another performance scaling axis, governed by a distinct logarithmic law. The authors focus on single-cell genomic models, where a dominant source of measurement noise is due to molecular undersampling.
- **Later version:** The author list expands to include Igor Sadalski, Dan Raviv, and Jonathan Rosenfeld, from Cellular Intelligence. The title changes to "A measurement noise scaling law for cellular representation learning." This version reports fitting 1,670 representation learning models across three data modalities (gene expression, sequence, and image data), and noise scaling follows a logarithmic law.
- **Draft manuscript:** A file named as a Nature Biotechnology draft carries the same title and authors. This suggests the paper was submitted to a Nature-family journal, but I found no confirmation of Nature Machine Intelligence or of a published version.

##### s42256-026-01321-w
# Abstract
Programmable design of RNA sequences with defined functions remains a central challenge in biology. Despite recent advances, existing RNA generative models lack robust controllable design capabilities and are constrained by short context windows, limiting their capacity to model the complex evolutionary manifold of full-length transcripts. Here we introduce EVA (Evolutionary Versatile Architect), a long-context generative RNA foundation model trained on over 114 million full-length RNA sequences spanning the full breadth of evolutionary diversity. By integrating a mixture-of-experts architecture with an 8,192-token context window, EVA learns a unified, evolution-consistent representation of the RNA sequence space that captures both global transcript structure and fine-grained functional elements. EVA establishes a unified framework for a broad spectrum of RNA design tasks within a single architecture, ranging from mutational fitness prediction to context-aware sequence engineering. We demonstrate EVA’s versatility through de novo design and targeted optimization of diverse RNA classes, including transfers RNAs, aptamers and CRISPR guide RNAs, as well as messenger RNA and circular RNA therapeutics. In wet-lab assays, our best designed aptamers improve both fluorescence intensity and binding affinity by roughly twofold over the positive control. In systematic evaluations, EVA achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven of nine established benchmarks, generating sequences with more than tenfold lower Kullback–Leibler divergence to natural RNA secondary-structure feature distributions than the previous open-source RNA generator.

##### s42256-026-01329-2
# Abstract
Generating proteins with the full diversity and complexity of functions found in nature is a grand challenge in protein design. Here we present protein diffusion transformer (ProDiT), a multimodal diffusion model that unifies sequence and structure modelling paradigms to enable the generation of proteins with computationally predicted functions at scale. Trained on sequences, three-dimensional structures and annotations for 128 million proteins across the evolutionary landscape, ProDiT generates diverse, novel proteins that are computationally predicted to preserve known active- and binding-site motifs and can be conditioned on a wide range of molecular functions, spanning 463 Gene Ontology terms. We introduce a diffusion sampling protocol to design proteins with multiple functional states, and illustrate this protocol by computationally scaffolding enzymatic active sites from carbonic anhydrase and lysozyme such that they are predicted to be deactivated by a calcium effector. Our results showcase the capacity of ProDiT to satisfy design specifications inaccessible to existing generative models, thereby expanding the protein design toolkit.

# Explore related subjects

Discover the latest articles and news in related subjects.

-

Machine learning

-

Protein design

-

Protein Structure Prediction and Function Analysis

# Main
Generative models trained on datasets of protein sequences or backbone structures have enabled major progress in de novo protein design 1 , 2 . Recently, structure diffusion models 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 have been developed to generate protein binders 3 , 5 or scaffold functional motifs 3 , 6 while fine-tuned protein language models 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 have been prompted to generate functional sequences with low sequence similarity to existing ones 7 , 11 , 13 . However, these existing paradigms focus on only structure or sequence in isolation and are therefore fundamentally incapable of capturing the complete functional landscape of natural proteins. Structure generative models require handcrafted specification of function in terms of a binding partner or functional motif 3 , depend on slow and specialized architectures adopted from protein structure prediction 14 , and are limited to the relatively scarce structural training data in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). However, sequence generative models cannot natively reason about sequence–structure–function relationships, have shown lower generation quality compared with structure generative models 9 , and have relied on fine-tuning 7 or complex prompting and filtering 11 to generate functional proteins. Neither family of approaches can target protein dynamics, a key feature of natural proteins, which often adopt multiple states to modulate their functions (for example, motor proteins, allosterically regulated enzymes, signalling proteins). We hypothesize that a generative model, efficiently trained at scale with a broad understanding of the protein functional space via both sequence and structure, would unlock many crucial protein design capabilities.
Here we present protein diffusion transformer (ProDiT), a framework that unifies structural and sequence generative modelling into a multimodal diffusion generative process, to enable these design capabilities. ProDiT leverages direct diffusion-based modelling of three-dimensional structural coordinates alongside amino acid tokens using a fast, scalable transformer architecture, eschewing the specialized architectures typically used for modelling protein structure 14 . Our model design allows scaling multimodal training across large protein datasets, expanding beyond the PDB to the 214 million available structures in AlphaFoldDB 15 and utilizing the full set of functional annotations in UniProtKB. Compared with previous multimodal protein generative models such as ProteinGenerator 16 , Multiflow 17 and ESM3 11 , ProDiT performs diffusion directly in the native state spaces of both sequence and structure with a simple transformer architecture, enabling fast, scalable multimodal training on 128 million proteins with functional annotations. Our formulation enables in silico generation quality that matches or exceeds that of specialized structure generative models, such as RFdiffusion 3 , across all sequence lengths while also significantly exceeding the sequence-generation quality of dedicated protein language models such as EvoDiff 9 . Notably, this performance is achieved with a relatively simple, compact model.
We explore ProDiT’s broad understanding of the protein sequence and structural landscape by conditioning generation on functional descriptors in the form of molecular-function Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Although previous studies have included similar annotation inputs in their training 7 , 11 , they do not report detailed evaluations of function-conditioned generation. We conduct comprehensive benchmarking of ProDiT across 915 diverse GO terms representing highly specific descriptions of protein function and find generations predicted as functional for 463 of these terms, including terms represented in less than 0.01% of training examples in UniProtKB. Many of these generations have only moderate structural similarity to known functional proteins (template modelling (TM)-score < 0.7), showing an ability to generalize across the structural landscape. We also build on techniques from image generative modelling for prompt adherence to further boost GO term adherence, a family of techniques not applicable to tokenized models such as ESM3. Structural alignments of our generations against known functional proteins indicate that generated structures reproduce the geometry of known active-site residues, despite low global sequence similarity. Our designs additionally recover binding residues to enzymatic cofactors, for example, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAD(P)+) for aldehyde dehydrogenase and coenzyme A (CoA) for malonyltransferase, suggesting a multifaceted understanding of protein function.
Leveraging ProDiT’s multimodal capabilities, we also develop a principled protocol for the design of dynamic, multistate proteins, derived from a novel interpretation of the sequence–structure–function paradigm based on probabilistic graphical models. When distinct motifs are provided for the desired output protein states, our protocol generates two separate structural scaffolds coupled to a common sequence in a single generative rollout. As such, our approach represents a major advance over previous protocols requiring brute-force sampling of plausible alternative conformations, previously thought necessary for such a protein design task 18 , 19 . We apply this capability to computationally scaffold active sites from carbonic anhydrase and lysozyme such that they are predicted to be modulated by calcium binding, an important step towards the design of custom and controllable enzymes.

# Results

# Multimodal generation of sequence and structure
We sought to develop a general framework that combines methods from protein language models and structure diffusion models to enable multimodal generation. To do so, ProDiT iteratively reverses two diffusion processes: one consisting of Gaussian noise added to the Cα coordinates of centred protein structures and the other consisting of random masking of the amino acid sequence (Fig. 1a and Methods ). # Abstract
Programmable design of RNA sequences with defined functions remains a central challenge in biology. Despite recent advances, existing RNA generative models lack robust controllable design capabilities and are constrained by short context windows, limiting their capacity to model the complex evolutionary manifold of full-length transcripts. In wet-lab assays, our best designed aptamers improve both fluorescence intensity and binding affinity by roughly twofold over the positive control. # Abstract
Generating proteins with the full diversity and complexity of functions found in nature is a grand challenge in protein design. Here we present protein diffusion transformer (ProDiT), a multimodal diffusion model that unifies sequence and structure modelling paradigms to enable the generation of proteins with computationally predicted functions at scale. Trained on sequences, three-dimensional structures and annotations for 128 million proteins across the evolutionary landscape, ProDiT generates diverse, novel proteins that are computationally predicted to preserve known active- and binding-site motifs and can be conditioned on a wide range of molecular functions, spanning 463 Gene Ontology terms. We introduce a diffusion sampling protocol to design proteins with multiple functional states, and illustrate this protocol by computationally scaffolding enzymatic active sites from carbonic anhydrase and lysozyme such that they are predicted to be deactivated by a calcium effector. Our results showcase the capacity of ProDiT to satisfy design specifications inaccessible to existing generative models, thereby expanding the protein design toolkit.

# Main
Generative models trained on datasets of protein sequences or backbone structures have enabled major progress in de novo protein design 1 , 2 . Recently, structure diffusion models 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 have been developed to generate protein binders 3 , 5 or scaffold functional motifs 3 , 6 while fine-tuned protein language models 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 have been prompted to generate functional sequences with low sequence similarity to existing ones 7 , 11 , 13 . However, these existing paradigms focus on only structure or sequence in isolation and are therefore fundamentally incapable of capturing the complete functional landscape of natural proteins. Structure generative models require handcrafted specification of function in terms of a binding partner or functional motif 3 , depend on slow and specialized architectures adopted from protein structure prediction 14 , and are limited to the relatively scarce structural training data in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). However, sequence generative models cannot natively reason about sequence–structure–function relationships, have shown lower generation quality compared with structure generative models 9 , and have relied on fine-tuning 7 or complex prompting and filtering 11 to generate functional proteins. Neither family of approaches can target protein dynamics, a key feature of natural proteins, which often adopt multiple states to modulate their functions (for example, motor proteins, allosterically regulated enzymes, signalling proteins). We hypothesize that a generative model, efficiently trained at scale with a broad understanding of the protein functional space via both sequence and structure, would unlock many crucial protein design capabilities.
Here we present protein diffusion transformer (ProDiT), a framework that unifies structural and sequence generative modelling into a multimodal diffusion generative process, to enable these design capabilities. ProDiT leverages direct diffusion-based modelling of three-dimensional structural coordinates alongside amino acid tokens using a fast, scalable transformer architecture, eschewing the specialized architectures typically used for modelling protein structure 14 . Our model design allows scaling multimodal training across large protein datasets, expanding beyond the PDB to the 214 million available structures in AlphaFoldDB 15 and utilizing the full set of functional annotations in UniProtKB. Compared with previous multimodal protein generative models such as ProteinGenerator 16 , Multiflow 17 and ESM3 11 , ProDiT performs diffusion directly in the native state spaces of both sequence and structure with a simple transformer architecture, enabling fast, scalable multimodal training on 128 million proteins with functional annotations. Our formulation enables in silico generation quality that matches or exceeds that of specialized structure generative models, such as RFdiffusion 3 , across all sequence lengths while also significantly exceeding the sequence-generation quality of dedicated protein language models such as EvoDiff 9 . Notably, this performance is achieved with a relatively simple, compact model.

content.content:
# Abstract
Large genomic and imaging datasets can be used to train models that learn meaningful representations of cellular systems. Across domains, model performance improves predictably with dataset size and compute budget, providing a basis for allocating data and computation. Scientific data, however, are also limited by noise arising from factors such as molecular undersampling, sequencing errors and image resolution. Here we introduce mutual information with auxiliary signals as a metric of representation model performance and study its scaling with noise. By fitting more than 2,000 representation learning models across three data modalities (gene expression, sequence and image data), we show that noise defines a distinct axis along which performance improves. Noise scaling follows a logarithmic law. We derive the law from a model of noise propagation, and use it to define noise sensitivity and model capacity as benchmarking metrics. We show that protein-sequence representations tolerate error rates in modern sequencing data, whereas single-cell transcriptomic models remain noise limited at current measurement signal-to-noise ratio levels. Within transcriptomic cell-state representation learning models, we find that transformer-based models are more noise robust but less performant than variational autoencoders. Noise scaling metrics may support future model evaluation and experimental design.

content.content:
# Abstract
Diffusion models promise to accelerate materials design by directly generating novel structures with desired properties, but existing approaches such as conditional generation typically require expensive and substantial labelled data (>10,000) and lack adaptability. Here we present MatInvent, a general and efficient reinforcement learning workflow that optimizes diffusion models for goal-directed crystal generation. By formulating equivariant denoising as a multistep decision-making problem, MatInvent leverages policy gradient with reward-weighted Kullback–Leibler regularization, including experience replay and diversity filters to enhance optimization efficiency and sample diversity. For single-objective designs, MatInvent rapidly converges to target values within 60 iterations (~1,000 property evaluations) across electronic, magnetic, mechanical, thermal and physicochemical properties. Furthermore, MatInvent achieves robust optimization in design tasks with multiple conflicting properties, successfully proposing low-supply-chain-risk magnets and high- κ dielectrics. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, MatInvent exhibits comparable or superior generation performance under specified property constraints while markedly reducing the demand for property computation. Compatible with diverse diffusion model architectures and property constraints, MatInvent could offer broad applicability in materials discovery.

# Drupal warns of new site takeover flaw exploited in attacks

By

# Sergiu Gatlan

- November 27, 2026

- 05:10 AM

- 0



The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites.



Last week, Drupal patched a remote code execution (RCE) flaw tracked as CVE-2026-132165 that allows anonymous users to take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.



While the security issue wasn't initially flagged as being abused in the wild, an update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting it one day after patches were released.



The new security issue (CVE-2026-136716 ), patched one week later, addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched and also lets attackers hijack vulnerable Drupal sites.

"However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state," Drupal said on Wednesday.



"This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised."



While it has yet to share further details regarding these attacks, Drupal warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised admins to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, and to consider resetting it.



They should also check site logs for unauthorized access, focusing on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account, and follow this guide if they find evidence the site may have been compromised.



Those who can't immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23 , 11.3.23 , or 11.4.14 should secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.



The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been exploited in ransomware attacks.

HTTP 200 · https://krebsonsecurity.com/feed/ · application/rss+xml
Krebs on Security
In-depth security news and investigation
Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:36:39 +0000
CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
Sat, 21 Nov 2026 00:36:39 +0000
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

- 86% of firms have adopted AI, up from 75% in 2024.
- 94% have at least one AI system in production.
- Nearly 9 in 10 use AI to improve enterprise productivity.
- Adoption among smaller firms remains among the lowest.

content.content:
The sector has been one of the fastest adopters of AI. The latest survey from the Bank and the FCA showed that 86% of firms have now adopted the technology, up from 75% in 2024.
94% of respondents had at least one AI system in production, while nearly 9 in 10 were using AI to improve enterprise productivity.
Fundamentally I see agentic payments as an opportunity for people across the UK; and we will work with organisations, with the regulator too to ensure those opportunities and benefits can be realised by UK consumers in a way that is safe and engenders trust.
Our existing regulatory framework provides a strong foundation. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum has set out how competition, consumer and data protection law, alongside online safety and cyber security requirements, apply to AI agents. And it’s now vital that we come together as Government, the financial services regulator, tech providers and the FS industry to work at pace on ensuring we strike the right regulatory balance between innovation and consumer protection – through a dedicated Agentic Policy Sprint.
And that ambition is why, in January, we appointed Harriet Rees and Dr Rohit Dhawan as our Financial Services AI Champions.
When speaking to the Champions, the industry reiterated its support for our principles-based, outcomes-focused regulatory framework.
We are now working with the AI Champions, industry and the regulators to deliver on these recommendations.
The two Champions have helped set an ambitious direction for AI in financial services. Their mandate for this next phase is clear: help us turn adoption into deployment, and deployment into scale.

British government takes services offline following ‘cyber incident’ | The Record from Recorded Future News
Services were taken down as a 'precaution' said the department

# British government takes services offline following ‘cyber incident’
Britain’s Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said Friday that it had experienced a cyber incident, with several services taken down as a precaution.
The nature of the incident has not been disclosed. In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for the DWP said the department had “taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident.”
The department is the largest in the British government by spending and administers the state pension and a range of other benefits. Millions of people in the country depend on its payments for essential bills.
“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal,” the spokesperson added.
The department said it was “working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption.”
The incident comes days after the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it has observed “a marked rise” since September in cyberattacks assisted by artificial intelligence.
Earlier this year, the British government acknowledged its yearslong approach to its own cybersecurity was flawed and warned it will be impossible to meet a previous target of securing all government organizations from known cyber vulnerabilities and attack methods by 2030.
“To protect our critical national infrastructure, defend public institutions and maintain public confidence in essential public services, we must achieve a radical shift in approach and a step change in pace,” it said at the time, warning the public sector faced a “critically high” cyber risk.
